Otherwise he sends an embassy, that is, consults a father of confession, and is reconciled with his body by taking lighter spiritual exercises that the body can bear, then gradually grows in his striving and spiritual exercises, with the spirit and body in agreement and at peace in the way of the Kingdom.

Christ lays down the third condition in spiritual striving, which is relying on God and not on the wealth of the world, so the spiritual person detaches himself from it and gives it to the needy, and is not disturbed if he loses some of it.

"Ears": the meaning is to hear with both ears, that is, with full attention; it also means by the two ears the outer ear and the inner ear in the heart, that is, spiritual understanding, and it means hearing His word, understanding it and applying it in life.

Salt keeps food from corruption and gives it a good taste; likewise the children of God are responsible for declaring the truth, doing good and keeping God's commandments. But if the salt (the children of God) loses its savor by mixing with the world and desires and by refusing to bear the cross and every spiritual striving, it will lose its saltiness and all its qualities, and then it is of no use and is cast into eternal torment; that is, the children of God who have abandoned their spiritual life and become absorbed in the world are condemned, and their judgment is harder.
If God has revealed to us the conditions of salvation, we must strive in them, confident of His love which upholds us and gives us the Kingdom.
The parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin and the prodigal son. The parable of the lost sheep (vv. 1-7):
This parable appears in (Mt 18:12-14).

1- Then drew near unto him all the publicans and sinners for to hear him. 2- And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, "This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them." 3- And he spake this parable unto them, saying, 4- What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it? 5- And when he hath found it, he layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing. 6- And when he cometh home, he calleth together his friends and neighbours, saying unto them, Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost. 7- I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance.
"Drew near unto him for to hear him": they felt their need to hear His teachings, in which there is hope for sinners of repentance and life with God.
"This man": they meant to belittle Christ because He mingled with sinners.
"Eateth with them": He went further in associating with sinners, and Christ meant by this to find a greater opportunity to teach them and draw them to repentance.

The Law provided for avoiding the wicked so that we do not share in their evils, but the Pharisees and scribes were excessive in carrying out the Law because of their pride, so they despised sinners and also those who collect taxes (the tax collectors), because tax collecting was linked with harshness, exploitation and love of money. They overlooked the importance of caring for sinners and drawing them to repentance; rather, in their excess they accused Christ of evil because He mingled with them, although Christ was concerned with calling sinners to repentance. Therefore He welcomed them and was able to draw some of them not only to repentance but to service, like St. Matthew the Evangelist, who was a tax collector.
Because love for sinners and compassion for them were far from the hearts of the Pharisees, Christ presented it to them in a parable, that perhaps they might understand and their hearts be softened.
"Until he find it": the shepherd does not rest but keeps looking for his lost sheep until he finds it and it returns to the fold.

The parable He gave is of a man who has a hundred sheep feeding in the wilderness where there is greenery, and when he returned with them to their fold he found one of them missing, so he left the ninety and nine and went out looking for the lost sheep. The shepherd signifies Christ, who left His ninety and nine sheep, who are the angels, in the fold, which is heaven, and became incarnate to seek Adam and his sons, "the lost sheep."

Here He makes clear the importance of the one soul that the shepherd or servant seeks, who is not preoccupied with the ninety and nine who are faithful to the Church, because the ninety and nine are secure in their holding fast to God, while the person who has strayed needs more than all.

When the shepherd found the lost sheep he did not rebuke it, since he found it worn out from its straying and long walking, so he carried it on his shoulders with love and pride because it has great value in his heart, and he returned with it to the fold and called those who love him to rejoice with him over the lost sheep that returned to live with its brothers.

Just as Christ carried our sins on His shoulders when He was hung on the cross, then went down to Hades and brought up Adam and his sons, and the angels rejoiced in Paradise at man's return to his first place with them, so the whole Church rejoices at the sinner's return, and the servant cares for him more than for all, to heal his wounds with which he was wounded in the period of his straying, as the members of the Church take care to welcome him.

Heaven rejoices at the sinner's return because he was lost, while the ninety and nine are at ease in their relationship with God. In addition, when the sinner returns he is eager to make up for what he missed, so he rushes along the spiritual way and may surpass those who did not stray like him, because of the slackness of some of them.

There is another interpretation, that the ninety and nine just persons are righteous in their own eyes, so they feel they do not need repentance, and therefore the heavenly ones rejoice over this one sinner because he is repentant. Do not be occupied with the many and forget the distant person, but give him of your love even if you grow very tired for his sake, and if he refuses your love do not forget him in your prayer, and repeat the attempt to seek him as much as you can bear.

entries.section: (2) The parable of the lost coin

paragraphs.text: Among His hearers were some shepherds, so He gave them the parable of the lost sheep, and He also found some women, so He gave the parable of the lost coin, to confirm the importance of the one soul in His sight and to call us to have compassion on sinners and those who are far.

A Jewish woman was given ten drachmas at her marriage, so they had more value for her than their ordinary value. If one of them was lost, she would look for it with concern and light her lamp to reveal some of the dark corners in her house, and not rest until she found it.
The woman signifies the Church.
The number ten signifies perfection.

The fall of man caused Christ to become incarnate, to shine by His life as a lamp for humanity and reveal to it the way of salvation by examining the aspects of its life (sweeping the house) through His holy teachings, and then to rescue it by His redemption on the cross and bring it back to Paradise.

How great is the duty of the servants in seeking the distant person in all the wanderings of life, and the duty of the fathers of confession in alerting souls to know their sins, so that they receive forgiveness and life in Christ.

entries.section: (2) The parable of the lost coin

paragraphs.text: The woman calls her friends to rejoice with her over the lost coin that she found, as the Church calls the triumphant part of it, that is, the heavenly ones, to rejoice at the return of sinners.

The Church's love and sense of responsibility appear in her saying that she "lost" it, although it is the person who strayed and refused life in the Church; but her love as a mother seeks after him out of her responsibility for his being lost, until she finds him. Do not be content with rebuking sinners, but first look at what love you have given them and what you can give now, for you are responsible for the return of these sinners, and with God's help you can bring them back to the Church's embrace.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: This parable is one of the most famous parables of Christ, showing God's love for sinners and His abundant gifts to them if they repent.
The younger son signifies the Gentiles, or the sinners and tax collectors among the Jews.
The elder son signifies the Jews, or the scribes and Pharisees, or the proud in general, especially those connected with the spiritual life.
The father signifies God.

In rebellion, contrary to custom, the son asked his father for his share of the inheritance and did not wait until his death. This means his neglect of enjoying his father's house, that is, the Church, and his lack of understanding of her care. The father, out of tenderness, agreed and gave him his share of the inheritance, and he took it and journeyed into a far country, which is selfishness.

Since this son loved himself more than he loved his father, he became estranged from the divine love through his falling into the self, and supposed that his happiness was in it and in satisfying its material desires.
"Wasted his substance": that is, all his energies, gifts and senses on the passing things of the world, until he squandered them wastefully without awareness.

The devil deceives you that freedom is satisfying your material desires, and makes you forget that you lose your sonship to God and His care for you. So obey the commandment to keep your sonship in the Church.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: The prodigal son was immersed in his desires and spent all the money he had until it ran out, and he found no food to sustain him. He was surprised by a famine throughout the country to which he had gone, and so he found no one to give him anything to eat, and he was forced to look for work to live from, and found only lowly work, which was feeding swine, which are marked by filthiness. His wage was small and did not suffice for his sustenance, so he longed to eat of the food of the animals he was feeding, which is the carob pods. When he tried to take something from them, the owner of the swine rebuked him, so he worked much and ate little, and became exposed to dying of hunger. So the prodigal son was occupied with the pleasures of the world, and at the end he discovered his hunger for righteousness; and instead of returning to his father (God), he again sought in the world for work in order to eat and be satisfied with these material things, and he found an employer, who is Satan, the prince of this world, who sent him to the works of the world, which are his fields, to feed swine. Swine were unclean and forbidden among the Jews, and raising them was not permitted because they represent uncleanness, that is, the works of the world connected with unclean desires.

And he found nothing in them to satisfy him, so his hunger increased until he needed to eat the food of the animals, which is the husks. The husks are hollow pods up to 30 cm long that hang from trees and are given to animals.
"No man gave unto him": that is, he needed evil and the hollow food that does not satisfy, that is, material things, and did not find it, and he nearly died of hunger and departed from life.
Satan lures you with the pleasure of desires until he humiliates you and leads you to destruction. So return quickly through repentance before Satan humiliates you.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: Here the greatness of repentance appears, and the secret of the strength of this prodigal son, who is also called the clever one, for he came to himself and discovered the results of his sin, which are humiliation and nearness to destruction, and compared himself with his glory in his father's house, and that the lowest person with his father, the hired servant and not the son of the house, has enough to eat and to spare. So he grieved in his heart for his former joy, standing and way of life.

He signifies the person who keeps away from the Church in the desires of the world and its various preoccupations, so he loses his joy and is deprived of his spiritual food; and when he is humbled by sin, God reminds him of his first life in the Church, and how the beginner in the spiritual life, whom the hired servant signifies, is spiritually satisfied, and indeed has many opportunities for spiritual food before him. So he longs for repentance and for returning to his sonship to God in the Church.

So he decided to return to his father and declare his repentance, that he had sinned against heaven and not only against his father, and with contrition he declares his unworthiness to return in the rank of sonship, but wishes that his father would receive him as a hired servant, that is, the lowest person in the Church.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: The love of the Father who awaits his son appears; when the son rose and began to move on the way of return, that is, repentance, he found his father running toward him in haste to embrace him and hold him close, not caring about the filthiness of his clothes and body, because God's love forgives all our sins and we become whiter than snow.

"And fell on his neck": he lifted from him the yoke of the slavery of sin and also showed his love and tenderness by this fatherly kiss. And when the son began to declare his confession, the father did not let him finish by allowing him to be a hired servant, but stopped him at his declaration of unworthiness of sonship, in order to give him, by his fatherhood, a complete sonship.
The tenderness of God is beyond all imagining, and He does not shrink from our sins but by His love lifts them from us and cleanses us from all our iniquities.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: God showed His fatherhood to His prodigal son by commanding His servants, that is, the priests in the Church, to put on him the best robe, which is the garment of righteousness that we receive in Baptism when our nature is renewed in it (Gal 3:27), or that we receive in the sacrament of repentance and confession; then the ring, which is the seal of the Holy Spirit in the sacrament of the Holy Myron, so that the Holy Spirit may dwell in us permanently (2 Cor 1:21, 22); as for his feet, He gave him shoes, which is walking by the word of God, which confirms sonship (Eph 6:15). The son wears shoes, but the hired laborer has none.

As for the fatted calf, it is the Lamb without blemish, Christ our God, who was slain on the cross for our redemption, and we eat Him as true Body and Blood on the altar every day and live by Him (Jn 6:56). And the father declared to all the members of his household that they should rejoice at the return of his prodigal son, who returned to life by his repentance and return to the Church through the Holy Sacraments.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: The elder son represents the Jews, or the proud, or those connected with God in appearance.
The field signifies the world, with which many are occupied.
"The house": that is, the Church.
"Musick and dancing": that is, the loud hymns of praise in the Church, in joy at the sinner's return and in thanksgiving to God.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: "He asked": that is, he read the Holy Bible.

"One of the servants": that is, one of the prophets of the Old Testament who prophesied the acceptance of the Gentiles in the salvation of Christ the Redeemer when they returned to Him in repentance and faith.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: The servant told the elder son of his prodigal brother's return and his father's joy over him because he had come back to the house. He signifies the prophets who wrote of the repentance of sinners and the acceptance of the Gentiles, or he signifies the priests and servants of the New Testament who declare the acceptance of repentant sinners in the Church and their partaking of the Holy Sacraments.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: The Jews, or the proud in the Church, were distressed and angry at the acceptance of the Gentiles and sinners, and refused to enter the house of God because of their pride.
"His father came out": the father's tenderness made him come out to them, seeking the salvation of the Pharisees and the proud Jews also.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: "Do I serve thee" these many years, with pride: the Pharisees suppose that they have a claim on God by their service to Him.

"Neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment": the Pharisees feel their self-righteousness and their complete application of the Law and commandments. The kid signifies the material desires of the world.
Pride made them ask for earthly goods and not spiritual food, while the repentant, humble prodigal son was united with Christ in the sacrament of the Eucharist.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: "This thy son": the proud dared to say to God of their brother "this thy son," disowning him.

"Hath devoured thy living": he wasted the gifts that were given to him, for they provoke God against their brothers the sinners. "With harlots": he accused his brother of consorting with harlots, although the parable did not mention this, but only that he wasted his substance; pride made him accuse his brother falsely.
Humble yourself so that your eyes may be enlightened and you rejoice at the sinner's acceptance and do not condemn him, and discover God's mercies, of which you are the most needy person.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: "Son": He showed His fatherhood to him despite his murmuring and his hatred of his brother, for God seeks the salvation of all, including the proud.
"All that I have is thine": true sonship has all the divine blessings, and this means that the elder son does not feel his sonship to God.

God declared a truth to the Jews and to all those connected with the Church, which is that He has given them His abundant goods and His sure promises, and they ought to have enjoyed them, so as not to fall into pride but to have their hearts opened to love for their brothers the sinners, and even to seek to bring them back and rejoice at their return. For as much as we grieve at a person's death in the body, we rejoice at anyone's rising from death, in the case of his repentance and return if he was a sinner, or his faith if he was not a believer. The parables of the unjust steward and of the rich man and Lazarus. The parable of the unjust steward (vv. 1-8):

1- And he said also unto his disciples, "There was a certain rich man, which had a steward; and the same was accused unto him that he had wasted his goods. 2- And he called him, and said unto him, How is it that I hear this of thee? give an account of thy stewardship; for thou mayest be no longer steward."

3- Then the steward said within himself, What shall I do? for my lord taketh away from me the stewardship: I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed. 4- I am resolved what to do, that, when I am put out of the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.
5- So he called every one of his lord's debtors unto him, and said unto the first, How much owest thou unto my lord? 6- And he said, An hundred measures of oil.

And he said unto him, Take thy bill, and sit down quickly, and write fifty. 7- Then said he to another, And how much owest thou? And he said, An hundred measures of wheat. And he said unto him, Take thy bill, and write fourscore. 8- And the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely: for the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: Christ gave His disciples a parable about the importance of preparing for eternity by faithfulness in our earthly life, which is the parable of the unjust steward. He tells us of a rich man who appointed a steward to manage his affairs, but the steward was not faithful and exploited his master's money to satisfy his desires. So he wasted and squandered this money, and some told his master of his steward's unfaithfulness.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: The master called his steward and confronted him with the charge of stealing his money, and demanded that he give an account of his stewardship because he would dismiss him from his work.

Prepare, my brother, for this moment when the demons accuse you, and God decides to end your life and demands that you give an account of all your past deeds, and even your words and thoughts. So take refuge in repentance every day and do everything you can to leave your sins, and you will receive forgiveness in the sacrament of confession; continue in the life of repentance and do not fear death.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: "Dig": that is, to dig the ground with a hoe.
"To beg": to ask alms.

The unfaithful steward thought about the decision of dismissal that he faced and what he would do after that: he could not work as an ordinary laborer, digging the ground with a hoe and farming it, since after having been the manager of all these properties he would become a simple laborer; and on the other hand he could not get his needs by begging and asking alms.

This steward who robbed his master said that he could not work as a laborer because he was lazy, and could not beg because he was proud. All these are bad traits, but the only virtue he had was that he thought carefully to solve his problem, and he arrived at wrong human solutions, namely robbing his master so that those who shared in the embezzlement would honor him after he was dismissed. He is wicked and his devices are wicked, but his distinction was in not giving in and in seeking a solution.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: His human thinking guided him to go further in robbing his master by giving up his rights to those who leased his land, that is, honoring these tenants at his master's expense. So he called one who was responsible for paying the master a hundred baths of oil each year (the bath is about 23 liters) and gave him the document or bill that established the master's right, for him to tear it up and write fifty instead; and so with another who was to give a hundred measures of wheat (the measure is about 230 liters), and he said to him, tear up the bill and write eighty; and so with the rest of the tenants. They rejoiced at this concession and promised to honor him after his dismissal from the stewardship.

entries.section: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

paragraphs.text: "Children of this world": the children of the world who walk in evil.
"Children of light": the children of God, who is the true light, and who walk in the light of God's commandments.

The master admired the wisdom of this wicked steward and commended him, not for his evil and treachery but for his wisdom in getting himself out of the problem of dismissal. It is clear that the one who commended him is his master in the parable and not Christ, because Christ does not commend evil.

And Christ commented that the wicked children of the world, who use theft and treachery to achieve their goals, care for their future more than the children of light, that is, the children of God, in their preparing for eternity by doing good and righteousness. Learn from the conduct of those around you, and acquire their virtues, and be careful not to fall into the conduct of the wicked, lest their painful fate confront you.
"Friends": those in material need and those far from God, whom you help so that they become children of God and therefore friends to you.

"Mammon of unrighteousness" is the wealth of the world, considering that its distribution among people is not just, since some are born rich and some poor, and considering that many material dealings are marred by unfaithfulness and injustice; therefore money in general is called the mammon of unrighteousness.
"Ye fail": you die and leave this life.
"They may receive you": they will have died before you, and they await you in the Kingdom.

"Everlasting habitations": the lasting heavenly Kingdom, to distinguish it from the temporary, passing tents and houses of the world. Christ continues His comment, advising His children to use the world and material things by giving them to the needy, and in this way they make friends for themselves with the wealth of the world, so that these friends may bear witness for the children of God in eternity to the good works they did, and they inherit the Kingdom of Heaven.
"That which is least" is the possessions of this earthly life.
"Much" is the bliss of eternal life.

Whoever is faithful in using his life on earth to do good, God entrusts him with the inheritance of the Kingdom of Heaven; but whoever uses the world for his desires and selfishness and wrongs the needy and does not help them is not entrusted with the inheritance of the Kingdom. This means that Christ confirms the importance of faithfulness and does not commend the treachery of the unjust steward, and calls us only to imitate his wisdom, so that we are faithful during our life on earth because we are stewards from God over our bodies and all our abilities, and afterward He gives us the Kingdom as a reward.

If the "unrighteous mammon" means the wealth of this world, then the "true riches" is the inheritance of the Kingdom of Heaven. That is, faithfulness is required in the earthly life so that God may give us the Kingdom of Heaven.

We are stewards over everything we have in our earthly life because it belongs to God, and our life is not for this world, but we are created for good works which God has before ordained for us (Eph 2:10). Material things are not ours; what is ours is the virtue and righteousness that we enjoy in eternity.

Christ declared a clear truth, which is the necessity of loving God with all the heart, and using the wealth of the world as a gift from God for doing good. But if a person is attached to money, he must leave God out of his heart and become a slave of money.
Examine yourself every day: was your aim in all your thoughts, words and deeds the love of God, or the love of the world and acquiring material things???

Christ directed His words to His disciples, but there were Pharisees listening to Him. The Pharisees were marked by the love of money, so the parable and Christ's comment on it showed their sin. Instead of repenting, they scoffed at His words, fulfilling Christ's saying that whoever serves money and is attached to it rejects the word of God, since the love of money leads to pride, so that a person supposes he is superior to others by the abundance of his money, although in God's sight he is a sinner, unfaithful in distributing his money to the needy.

Christ boldly rebuked the Pharisees, because they were concerned with exalting themselves before the Jews, saying that this changes nothing because God knows the truth of your hearts, wicked and unclean with the love of pride and the love of money; for they refused to acknowledge their sin, which was the love of money, but justified themselves and neglected the work of mercy, and even supposed themselves better than those around them and the most deserving of people for the Kingdom.
Remember that you are a steward over all that you have, so use it to do good, and offer repentance in humility for every shortcoming, and God will guide you how to use your life to help the needy.

entries.section: (4) The importance of the commandment, and divorce

paragraphs.text: "The law and the prophets were until John": all the teachings of the Old Testament from Moses until John the Baptist.
"Since that time": that is, after John the Baptist, and it means the proclamation of Christ.

The passing away of heaven and earth is an impossible matter because they are fixed throughout the days. This means that the Law and all the teachings of Christ are fixed throughout life, so we must submit to them and not scoff at them as the Pharisees did. "One tittle": the smallest teaching in the Old Testament.

Christ declares that His proclamation is the completion and extension of the books of the Old Testament and its prophecies, and the necessity of adhering to all the commandments; even if they are difficult in appearance, a person should hold to them and force himself to keep them, and not walk by his own desires, striving to reach the eternal Kingdom, which is better than every earthly desire.

entries.section: (4) The importance of the commandment, and divorce

paragraphs.text: This verse is mentioned in (Mt 5:31-32; 19:3-9). Since Christ showed the importance of God's commandments, He confronted the evil of the Pharisees who pretended to hold to them but permitted divorce for trivial reasons, such as the wife's not serving a suitable meal so that her husband divorces her. As an example of the permanence of God's commandments He declared the commandment of marriage, which preserves the structure of the family. Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, because the first marriage still stands, and the husband left it for his own purposes, making light of the holy sacrament which the Holy Spirit accomplished. So his second marriage is invalid even if it has civil legitimacy; rather it is adultery in the sight of God and the Church. And if a man marries a divorced woman he commits adultery, because she is still in God's sight bound to her first husband, unless the divorce was for the cause that Christ declared, namely the adultery of the other party, in which case the innocent party has the right to marry. Do not distort God's word and be careless of His commandments for your own purposes, using your philosophy, but humble yourself and force yourself to keep the commandment even if it seems heavy, and God will uphold you and comfort your heart and give you in the end eternal life.

entries.section: (5) The parable of the rich man and Lazarus

paragraphs.text: "Sumptuously every day": continuing in material desires and being immersed in them.

Christ gave a parable about the work of mercy and enduring suffering as a way of preparing for the Kingdom, saying: there was a rich man who was concerned with his clothing and his pleasures and desires, which He expressed by the garments of kings, that is, purple and fine linen, and he was immersed in everything the soul desires of food, drink, comfort and possessions in his great palace, with singing and dancing, and all you can imagine of the luxury of this world. He did not commit evident sins against God's commandments, but his sin was being absorbed in material things and the pleasures of the world.

entries.section: (5) The parable of the rich man and Lazarus

paragraphs.text: "Was laid": that is, some of his acquaintances placed him before the rich man's palace, perhaps that he would have pity on him with food and treatment; this means that he was unable to move and needed someone to carry him.
"Sores": as a result of his inability to move, and his being among filth, he was exposed to microbes, so his skin peeled and blood flowed from it.

"Desiring to be fed": wishing to eat something of the rich man's scraps, but even this trivial thing that they might throw out with the garbage was not available to him; yet one of the servants in the palace may have carried some crumbs to him without the rich man's knowledge, or when the scraps were thrown outside the palace some of them were beside him and he ate a little of them.

"The dogs came": the dogs came to eat from the scraps, and found the blood flowing from his almost naked body, so they hurried to lick the sores because they love blood, and so they moistened the sores and eased his pains a little; they had more pity on him than the rich man.

At the gate of the palace of this great rich man lived a poor, naked man stricken with diseases. The rich man was occupied with his pleasures and did not feed this poor man or treat his diseases, and the poor man did not find his necessary food; he longed for the scraps thrown from the rich man's palace and found only a little of them, and for his sores he found no physician or anyone who cared for him. So it was the dogs that licked his sores and moistened them, and the poor man bore being food for the dogs that licked his blood, as he also bore all his poverty with thanksgiving and patience.

The poor man's name was "Lazarus," that is, "God is my help," so God's help upheld him so that he bore it, and he deserved to be called by name; but the rich man, because of the meanness of his life far from God, was not given a name in the parable. From the parable we sense the enormous difference between the conditions of the rich man and Lazarus in the following:-
1- The rich man wears the finest clothes, and Lazarus is naked with his sores uncovered.
2- The rich man is immersed in the desires of food and drink, and Lazarus longs for a little of the scraps of the rich man's food.
3- Many serve the rich man, and Lazarus finds no one who cares for him except the dogs that came to lick his blood, not out of love for him but because he became food for them.

The rich man signifies those occupied with the desires of the world rather than the work of mercy and the love of God; for if he had loved prayer and been bound to God he would have loved the needy and helped them.

He also signifies the Jewish people, who received the knowledge of God in the commandments and the Law, but neglected to convey it to the Gentiles, and even despised them and was vexed by their evident sins, like sores, and left them in their poverty.

As for Lazarus, he signifies those who bear the afflictions of life with thanksgiving, and the Gentiles who lived in poverty and the diseases of sin for many years, but declared and confessed their sins, since sores bring blood out from inside the body to the outside, that is, confessing the inner sin openly, and so they received God's mercies in the blood of Christ the Redeemer. May you feel the needs of those around you, not only for food and material treatment but rather those far from God who suffer from sin, because they need you to show them your love and make them know a little about God, so that they are satisfied by Him and are at ease in His hands. Do not be selfishly absorbed in your wrong preoccupations, for you are responsible for offering love to all around you, and you are a steward over God's gifts and the abilities given to you, to distribute them to the needy.

entries.section: (5) The parable of the rich man and Lazarus

paragraphs.text: "The beggar died": no concern for burying his body is mentioned; rather he died where he was without anyone's concern, but heaven hastened to welcome him.

Abraham's bosom represents all the saints rejoicing in heaven, and he is a great father to the people of God and to everyone in the world who believes. Abraham's being in Paradise before the redemption was accomplished on the cross does not trouble us, because it is a parable and not an actual story, and it expresses what will happen after the redemption is accomplished.

"The rich man also died, and was buried": people were concerned with the funeral and burial of the rich man, but his spirit found no place except in torment. The rich man's soul died because of his distance from God and his preoccupation with bodily desires, so the death of his body and his burial were a natural extension of the former death of his soul. As for Lazarus, who bore all the sufferings patiently, when he had fulfilled his labors he was taken to heaven full of many virtues, and was heavy from the abundance of virtues he carried, so he needed many angels to carry him to Paradise, to enjoy being with God and the saints. So Lazarus, who signifies the Gentiles, was in Abraham's bosom, because he believed in Christ and accepted his sufferings with thanksgiving; but the rich man, who signifies the Jews, because of his selfishness went far from his father Abraham, the father of faith, and was cast into hell and eternal torment.

entries.section: (5) The parable of the rich man and Lazarus

paragraphs.text: "He lifted up his eyes": confirms that hell is in a lower place and Paradise in a lofty place; this is in the moral sense and not the material, that is, Paradise is an exalted state and hell a low state. "Afar off": declares this distance between Paradise, the place where the righteous wait, and hell, the place where the wicked wait. As a result of this rich man's selfishness and his immersion in material desires, he was cast into hell, the place where the wicked wait after this life, and there he faced severe torment, expressed by the flame and the severe pain in his tongue and by its being a lower place; and he lifted up his eyes to Paradise, the place where the righteous wait, and found Lazarus enjoying himself in Abraham's bosom, with whom all the Jews hope to be in Paradise, and he asked for even a drop of water from Lazarus's finger to cool his tongue. This rich man who was stingy toward Lazarus with the crumbs that fell from his table became a beggar and did not receive.

A person's tongue is what leads him to eternal happiness or eternal torment, and because of the rich man's great arrogance and his much talk about material desires, his tongue suffered severe pain as he called out to Abraham, "Father Abraham," but he had lost his sonship by his evil and was in torment.

entries.section: (5) The parable of the rich man and Lazarus

paragraphs.text: Abraham's reply to the rich man was that the torment he suffers is his natural recompense, because he was immersed in material desires and made himself independent of the knowledge of God by them, while Lazarus bore the calamities with thanksgiving from God's hand, and so deserved comfort and eternal joy.
If you bear sufferings with thanksgiving, or lose some material things, do not be disturbed, because God compensates you for them in heaven.

entries.section: (5) The parable of the rich man and Lazarus

paragraphs.text: Abraham gave another reason for not granting his request, which is that there is a gulf between hell and Paradise that prevents anyone from passing from one to the other. This means that the condition in heaven is fixed, either in torment or in bliss, and there is no mixing between the righteous and the wicked, but they see one another, so the righteous are comforted and thank God when they see the torment of the wicked, and the torment of the wicked increases if they look at the happiness of the righteous, from which they are deprived forever.

entries.section: (5) The parable of the rich man and Lazarus

paragraphs.text: After the rich man despaired of having his pains eased, he made another request of Abraham, which was to send Lazarus to the earth to warn the rich man's five brothers so that they would repent, because they walk like their brother and are absorbed in material pleasures, that they might not come to the place of torment. By his request the rich man wanted his torment not to increase by seeing his brothers with him in hell, especially since he may have been a cause of their absorption in desires, because he was an example to them.
The five brothers signify the five senses, which, if they are not sanctified in Christ, are immersed in desires and lead a person to eternal torment.

entries.section: (5) The parable of the rich man and Lazarus

paragraphs.text: From the preceding dialogue it appears that those who have departed, even the wicked among them who are in hell, see those on earth and wish their salvation by repentance and life with God, but Abraham's reply to the rich man was that they have the books of the Old Testament, and this shows the importance of the Old Testament for a person's salvation and repentance. This parable also answers the heresy of the transmigration of souls, which proclaims that the spirit is incarnated in several bodies until it is purified of its sins and rises to the higher spirit. For instead of the rich man's being tormented, he could have been incarnated in a lowly body, as this heresy says.

entries.section: (5) The parable of the rich man and Lazarus

paragraphs.text: The rich man said to Abraham that the rising of one from the dead would alert those careless about the salvation of their souls to repent, but Abraham objected, declaring that whoever does not repent by reading the Holy Bible will not benefit from the rising of one from the dead, because the word of God, that is, Christ who is in the Scripture, is stronger than all for whoever wants to hear. Lazarus the brother of Mary and Martha rose from the dead when Christ raised him, and the Jews did not repent but tried to kill him; and likewise Christ rose from the dead and they did not repent either, but persecuted His disciples.
Take care to read the Holy Bible every day and obey it as a personal message to you from God.
How we prepare for the end of the days. Offences (vv. 1-2):

1- Then said he unto the disciples, "It is impossible but that offences will come: but woe unto him, through whom they come! 2- It were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and he cast into the sea, than that he should offend one of these little ones.

entries.section: (5) The parable of the rich man and Lazarus

paragraphs.text: Christ declares, by His foreknowledge, that stumbling blocks exist in the world, that is, that a person may draw another away from God's way, whether through heresy, a bad idea, a bad example, psychological pressures, persecutions, and so on. But Christ warns of woes, that is, severe torment, for everyone who causes another to stumble, because he does not sin only against God but also leads others away and makes them fall.

entries.section: (5) The parable of the rich man and Lazarus

paragraphs.text: This verse is also mentioned in (Mt 18:1). The little ones are any person who is weak in faith or knowledge or in any circumstance of weakness. Therefore God emphasizes the destruction of the one who causes them to stumble, expressing it by a heavy stone hung around his neck, which is the millstone with which grain is ground, and by his being cast into the sea, where he must sink and perish. That is, it would be better for him to perish before he causes another to stumble, because if he causes another to stumble, severe torment awaits him in the next life.
Examine your words, your actions and your appearance, even your laughter, lest you hurt the feelings of some and make them fall into sin.

Christ draws our attention to a clear stumbling block, which is unforgiveness, and He calls us to deal with any wrong done by someone by rebuking him. In (Mt 18:15) He instructs that the rebuke should be away from the eyes of others so as not to shame him; and if he repents, he is forgiven, but if he does not repent, he is forgiven in the heart so that he may receive God's forgiveness, as we pray in the Lord's Prayer, "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Yet the relationship between them may become very limited, or the wrongdoer may cut it off, so that there is no dealing between them at all; but the spiritual person keeps his peace, his love for him and his prayers for him.

Christ instructs us that if the wrong is repeated many times by the same person, up to seven times a day, and seven is the number of perfection, that is, however often his wrongs are repeated, there must be tolerance and forgiveness. If God rested on the seventh day, then your rest is to forgive your brother however much he wrongs you, just as God forgives you however much you sin every day.

A grain of mustard seed: a small black seed used as a spice. When it grows it becomes a tree reaching a height of three and a half meters, with large, firm roots. As a common Jewish expression, it denotes very small things...

The disciples asked Christ to increase their faith. He told them that true, living faith, even if it is small like a grain of mustard seed, is able to uproot a huge tree such as the sycamine, with roots spread out and strong in the earth, and plant it in the sea; that is, it works miracles and nothing is impossible before it.
The sycamine tree points to Satan or to sin rooted deep in the heart, and faith is able to be rid of it and of its authority and to drown it in the sea.

The natural custom to which people were accustomed, when their servants returned from their work in the field or from tending the flock, was that the servants would complete their household tasks of preparing supper for their master, and then eat themselves, not resting before finishing their work. So there is no merit for the servant in preparing his master's supper; it is his duty. Therefore none of us should boast of any good work he does, for this is a duty toward God, his Master, who bought him with His blood.
Gird yourself: tie up your loose garments so that you may be able to serve. This signifies spiritual striving throughout life.
Afterward: that is, in eternal life.
Eat and drink: the happiness and spiritual satisfaction in the Kingdom.

Spiritually, work in the field or tending the flock signifies the material works of the world in which God blesses us. But as we rise by returning to the house of our Master, which is the Church, we prepare supper for Him through service and preaching to those who are far off, and He eats and drinks the repentance and confession of those who were far away; and after this He grants us the heavenly food in eternal life.
The servant has no merit in fulfilling his duties, because he was bought with a price and ought to do his duty.

Likewise we must feel that we are God's servants; if we do all righteousness, this is our duty, and we should even consider ourselves unprofitable servants, because we fall short in our works, and God covers us and completes what we lack, and in His love even grants us the grace of sonship. Consequently, no one may claim to have extra virtues that he can give to others.

Note: Our Catholic brethren believe in a strange teaching called "the surplus merits of the saints." By this they mean that the great saints offered more virtues than God asked of them, and that it is their right as saints to give some people from this surplus credit, to make up for their deficiencies and shortcomings. This is a strange teaching which our Church rejects, because no human being has merit or surplus before God... and therefore we call this strange teaching "the heresy of the surplus merits of the saints."
If you do any righteousness or service, thank God humbly because He granted you to do this good work.

entries.section: (5) The healing of the ten lepers

paragraphs.text: Christ was heading toward Jerusalem to accomplish our redemption on the Cross, and because He came for the salvation of the whole world, He passed through Galilee and Samaria, which were full of Gentiles, to preach to all and save them. He headed toward a small village in Samaria, for He seeks the needy, even those whom people do not care about, and He found ten lepers living outside the village. For although this disease was bodily, in the form of spots appearing on the skin, in the Old Testament it indicated the uncleanness of its sufferer, and if anyone was struck with it, the Law required that he live apart outside the city, tear his clothes, not cover his head with a turban, cover his mustache, and cry out to everyone who approached him, "Unclean, unclean."
All these were signs of shame so that they might lead him to repentance.
The meaning of this is that sin keeps a person away from enjoying membership in the Church and the blessings God gives His children in the Church.

entries.section: (5) The healing of the ten lepers

paragraphs.text: These ten had heard of Jesus, His miracles and His teachings. Therefore, when they saw Him from afar, they believed in His power to heal them, and they cried out to Him, asking for His mercy to heal them.

entries.section: (5) The healing of the ten lepers

paragraphs.text: Christ did not heal them but commanded them to go and show themselves to the priests. The Law of Moses required that a leper who was healed go to the priest to be certain of it, offer a sacrifice, and be given a certificate of his cleanness.
The faith of these ten appeared in their obedience to Christ, for they went to the priests, and because of their obedience, while on their way, they were cleansed of their leprosy.

Do you obey God's commandments, confident of their power before you see their blessing and touch it? Persevere in your spiritual striving and in carrying out God's commandments even if you find no consolations, and trust that you will finally receive blessings that cannot be expressed.

entries.section: (5) The healing of the ten lepers

paragraphs.text: Glorified God: he believed that Jesus was from God, so he glorified God and declared his strong faith in Him by glorifying with a loud voice.
Fell down on his face: he prostrated himself before Him, in faith in His power and that He was from God.

A Samaritan: from the inhabitants of the northern kingdom. His origin was Jewish, but he had mixed with the Gentiles and had turned away from worshiping God in His temple at Jerusalem, so he was despised by the Jews. But what joined him with the nine Jews was their sharing in the disease of leprosy, which was regarded as uncleanness in everyone's eyes and a reason for their isolation outside the cities.
These ten were Jews, but one of them was a Samaritan, that is, from the group despised by the Jews because they did not hold fast to all the laws of Moses.

The nine set off, rejoicing in their healing, to meet the priests and their relatives and to return to their normal life. But this Samaritan felt that the first thing he ought to do was to thank Christ who had healed him, so he returned to Him rejoicing exultantly, prostrated himself before Him humbly, and thanked Him for His love for him.

entries.section: (5) The healing of the ten lepers

paragraphs.text: Christ wanted to show the distinction of this Samaritan, so He asked where the nine who were cleansed were, and why they did not return to give thanks. Then He praised this Samaritan, declaring the superiority of his faith, not only in obedience but in thanksgiving and glorifying God. Thus the despised foreign Samaritan became better than the Jews who knew the Law. "Thy faith hath made thee whole" not only from the disease of leprosy but from sins and immersion in lusts, because his heart loved God, and this appeared in his thanksgiving.
Are you careful to thank everyone who helps you and does you a service, even if it is small? And do you thank God in your prayers for His daily gifts to you?

entries.section: (6) The Kingdom of God within the soul

paragraphs.text: With observation: that is, with signs in the sky or human movements in a great reception of the Messiah. There are no material matters that I declare to you to watch for, because it is a spiritual kingdom over hearts. Lo here: that is, in Samaria or Galilee, the Christ appears.
Lo there: that is, in Jerusalem, where the temple of God is.
The kingdom of God is within you: that is, in your hearts, for God wants to reign over the hearts of His children. It also means within you, that is, in your midst.

The Pharisees asked Him about the time of the coming of the Kingdom, and their intent was the earthly kingdom of the Messiah. So He informed them not to be preoccupied with watching for external signs of the Kingdom, because it is a spiritual kingdom, and it is God's reign over the heart. Therefore He said, "Behold, the kingdom of God is within you," through the soul's faith and obedience to Christ, so that He reigns over it and gives it the joy of His fellowship until it reaches the heavenly Kingdom.

Take care of your personal relationship with Christ through your prayers and your readings until you feel His dwelling within you, and do not be preoccupied with His material blessings, for they are meant to lead you to love Him and to bind your heart to Him.

entries.section: (7) The signs of the end of the days

paragraphs.text: Christ spoke with His disciples about the signs of the end of the world, and foretold that it would bring many afflictions and that people would long for Christ to be with them to help them face these. But sadly they will not understand the signs, since they will be immersed in lusts and the thoughts of the world. But if they repent and live by faith, the Holy Spirit will work in them as Christ worked and helped His disciples during His days on earth.

entries.section: (7) The signs of the end of the days

paragraphs.text: Christ declared to His children that deceivers would appear saying that Christ has come in His second coming in some place in the world, but He warned them against believing these lies, because He will appear to all mankind at one time. And He gave an illustration of His second coming, which is the appearance of lightning, which moves swiftly from one end of heaven to the other and is seen by all at one time.

entries.section: (7) The signs of the end of the days

paragraphs.text: Then He alerted His disciples to the necessity that Christ first suffer and be crucified by the hands of the Jews (in this generation) and die for the redemption of mankind, and rise from the dead, and only after this come in His second coming.

entries.section: (7) The signs of the end of the days

paragraphs.text: Christ describes the days before His second coming as being like the days before the flood of Noah, and the days of Sodom before it was burned in the time of Lot, when people were occupied with their worldly affairs, far from God and from repenting of their sins, and suddenly the flood came or fire fell upon Sodom.

So also Christ will come in His second coming suddenly, while people are distracted from Him by the lusts of the world and its passing concerns, and He will hold them to account, and none will escape except the righteous children of God.

entries.section: (7) The signs of the end of the days

paragraphs.text: Christ warns His believing children not to give up their spiritual elevation (he who is on the housetop) by seeking and being immersed in the lusts of the world; and whoever strives, advancing in the way of the spiritual life and the service of the Lord (working in the field), must not return to his old lusts and material attachments like Lot's wife, who perished because her heart was attached to material things and she looked back.

So whoever gives up these material things that all the world seeks saves his soul; that is, the one who seems to be wearying and destroying himself by not caring for his body's comfort and luxury is the one who saves his soul and receives blessed eternity.

entries.section: (7) The signs of the end of the days

paragraphs.text: Christ makes clear that His children who live in the midst of the world He will take to Himself, and He will leave the wicked to eternal torment.

The two on the bed signify the rich; those grinding at the mill signify those who work hard in their worldly life, that is, the poor and the toilers; and the two in the field signify the priests and servants working in the vineyard of the Lord.
From these three categories there will be righteous and wicked, so the one is taken to the Kingdom and the other to eternal torment.

entries.section: (7) The signs of the end of the days

paragraphs.text: The body signifies the crucified Christ.
The eagles are God's believing children who eat the Body and Blood of the Lord in the Church and live.
There is another view, that the body signifies Satan, who is in torment, and around him the wicked gather to be tormented forever.
From all the foregoing, we must be vigilant to repent of every sin, to guard against wicked lusts, and to care for the love of God.
The parable of the unjust judge, the Pharisee and the tax collector, the love of money, the healing of the blind man. The parable of the unjust judge (vv. 1-8):

1- And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint; 2- saying, "There was in a city a judge, which feared not God, neither regarded man: 3- and there was a widow in that city; and she came unto him, saying, Avenge me of mine adversary. 4- And he would not for a while: but afterward he said within himself, Though I fear not God, nor regard man; 5- yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me." 6- And the Lord said, "Hear what the unjust judge saith. 7- And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them? 8- I tell you that he will avenge them speedily. Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?"

entries.section: (7) The signs of the end of the days

paragraphs.text: The human being doubts whether his prayer is answered, or grows weary of it through weakness of his love for God, and he may reject persistence in prayer with a rational philosophy that God knows everything, so why the repetition? So Christ wanted to show the importance of pressing upon God in prayer, because this builds up a person's faith and shows how great his love for Him is.

entries.section: (7) The signs of the end of the days

paragraphs.text: A judge: responsible for ruling justly and for vindicating the wronged.
Feared not God: there is no motive in his heart to hold to justice in order to please God.
Regarded not man: he takes no account of the opinion of society, and so there is nothing that calls him to justice for the sake of public opinion.
A widow: represents the person who has no support, so she is easily wronged.
She came: her repeated resorting to the judge to ask his help with a just verdict.
Avenge me of mine adversary: she had an adversary who persisted in obstructing her from obtaining her rights.

The parable says that there was an unjust judge in one of the cities, who took no account of God or men, being proud and regarding no one. And in the same city there was a widow, that is, a weak woman without support, who asked this judge to avenge her and give her her lost right.

entries.section: (7) The signs of the end of the days

paragraphs.text: He would not for a while: he neglected her case and did not rule justly.
Troubleth me: her persistent pressing annoys me.
Weary me: she presses upon me with her importunity.
Because of the woman's persistence, this unjust judge was compelled to vindicate her so that she would not trouble him, and not out of sympathy for her or adherence to justice.

entries.section: (7) The signs of the end of the days

paragraphs.text: Hear what he saith: note what this judge said, that he would vindicate the widow because of her much importunity.
Shall not avenge: shall not return to them their rights stolen by the devil, their adversary, giving them His peace and delivering them from sin, so that they even trample the power of Satan.
His elect: God's children whom He chose out of the world because of their response to Him.
Which cry: fervent, strong prayers.
Day and night: importunity and continuing in prayer.

Though he bear long with them: God postpones the answer for a time so as to give the gift at the best time, in order to build up the faith, the love and the striving of His children; but He does not forget them, and He must vindicate them in the end and grant them His abundant gifts. If an unjust judge responds to the importunity of the wronged woman, how much more will the just and loving God respond to His children when they press upon Him in prayer, to rescue them from the wicked and from the devil's wars.

entries.section: (7) The signs of the end of the days

paragraphs.text: I tell you: an affirmation of what follows.

Speedily: He will not be late beyond the proper time according to His wisdom for the benefit of His children, but at the best time He grants them His gifts, especially if we look at the short span of life in comparison with eternity.
Here Christ affirms the importance of linking importunity in prayer with faith, and He asks whether at His second coming He will find strong faith in many, that is, fervent prayers with importunity.
Believe that God hears your prayers even if He delays in answering, and continue in prayer to show your love for Him and your clinging to Him.

entries.section: (2) The Pharisee and the tax collector

paragraphs.text: Despised others: those who are proud fall easily into condemning and even despising others. Christ confronted a group of proud people who walked in the spiritual life with exactness but felt their own self-righteousness, so He gave them a parable through which He taught them the importance of humility.

entries.section: (2) The Pharisee and the tax collector

paragraphs.text: The parable shows that all are human beings in God's sight, whatever their position, but the evaluation is according to their spiritual life and their humility. The purpose of both was prayer, and this is a holy purpose, but what matters most is how one prays.

One of them was of the Pharisees, who held fast to the Law but felt their distinction and their righteousness over others. As for the tax collector, his conduct in life was evil, bound up with love of money and harshness toward others; but the good part was that he wanted to pray and to have a relationship with God.

entries.section: (2) The Pharisee and the tax collector

paragraphs.text: As other men: he puts himself in a high rank and the rest of the people in a low rank because of their evils.

The Pharisee began his prayer with thanksgiving, which is a beautiful thing, but it appeared from his thanksgiving that he felt his superiority, and even condemned people in general who had fallen into sins such as robbery, injustice and adultery; and more than this, he specifically condemned a man like himself, the tax collector who had entered to pray alongside him.

entries.section: (2) The Pharisee and the tax collector

paragraphs.text: The Pharisee continued his prayer, puffed up with his self-righteousness in fulfilling the commandments such as fasting and giving tithes.

entries.section: (2) The Pharisee and the tax collector

paragraphs.text: But the other person, the tax collector, felt his many sins and that he was unworthy to pray and to be in the house of God. So he stood afar off, looking at the temple with reverence and humility, and even smote his breast, declaring his remorse and repentance for all his former sins, humbly asking God's mercy and forgiveness and confessing his sins by saying, "the sinner."

The Pharisee signifies the Jewish nation, proud of its knowledge of God and His laws, while the tax collector signifies the sinful Gentiles who come humbly to Christ and so receive salvation, unlike the proud among the Jews.

entries.section: (2) The Pharisee and the tax collector

paragraphs.text: I tell you: an affirmation of the importance of what follows.
This man: the tax collector.
The other: the Pharisee.

The answer of heaven came in forgiveness of the humble tax collector's sins and his justification from every sin, while the proud Pharisee's prayer was rejected and even became a judgment upon him and a fixing of his sins on his head.

Then Christ our God comments on the parable, that whoever exalts himself and is proud, God rejects him and brings him down to hell, but whoever humbles himself in repentance and contrition, God honors him and exalts him to enjoy with Him the heavenly Kingdom.

Look at your sins and your weakness and you will be humbled before God, and this will move you to a strong relationship with Him in which you make up for what you have missed, and you will also look at the virtues of those around you in order to imitate them.

Some people from the crowds wanted their children to receive a blessing from Christ, so they brought them to Him that He might touch them. But the disciples felt that Christ's stature was too great for Him to care about children, so they tried to keep them away so that they would not distract their Teacher from His teachings and His healing of the sick by this trivial matter.

Christ cared for the children, and told His disciples to let the children come to Him, and He blessed them; and He even declared an important truth, namely the distinctiveness of children in their character from adults, and that those who have these traits of innocence, love for others, and appreciation of the care of those around them (as a child rejoices in the love of his parents and their gifts to him), are those qualified to enter the Kingdom of Heaven.
He did not say "of these children" but "of such," that is, those among adults who have the character of children, and not only children.
And we ought to care for the weak, for they too are in need, like children.
Also mentioned in (Mt 18:3). Christ affirmed the importance of acquiring the character of children as a condition for entering the Kingdom.
Consider the qualities of the children close to you and try to learn something from them, for God has placed them in your path not only for you to teach them but also for you to learn from them.

entries.section: (4) The love of money and entering the Kingdom of Heaven

paragraphs.text: A young Jewish man came forward, as the Gospels of Matthew and Mark relate, and he was a ruler of one of the synagogues of the Jews. He asked Christ how he might inherit eternal life, and addressed Him respectfully, saying, "Good Master."

entries.section: (4) The love of money and entering the Kingdom of Heaven

paragraphs.text: Before Christ answered his question, He asked him, "Why callest thou me good?" Are these words of reverence which some say without understanding, or do you mean that I am God, since "none is good, save one, that is, God"? Christ intends here to make the young man confront himself: does he believe in the divinity of Christ, so that he asks Him to make known to him the way to the Kingdom of Heaven; or is He in his eyes merely one of the teachers of the Jews; or is he testing Him, to see whether He will guide him according to the Law of Moses or contrary to it, so as to catch Him in an error.

entries.section: (4) The love of money and entering the Kingdom of Heaven

paragraphs.text: Christ did not state new commandments, because He came to fulfill and not to destroy, and He directed this ruler to keep the Ten Commandments; and to confirm that He meant these commandments and not other new ones that Christ teaches, He gave him examples of them, namely "Do not commit adultery, Do not kill"...

entries.section: (4) The love of money and entering the Kingdom of Heaven

paragraphs.text: The ruler answered quickly, declaring that he had kept the commandments from his youth. He means keeping them in the mind and literal application, and not all the depths of the commandments, as shown by the appearance afterward of his attachment to material things more than love for God, and this is contrary to the spirit of the commandments.

entries.section: (4) The love of money and entering the Kingdom of Heaven

paragraphs.text: Christ asked him to sell his possessions and distribute the price to the poor, and to follow Christ, depending on Him alone and not on his money. Christ directed this ruler's gaze to the heavenly treasure which he would gain by works of mercy, better than earthly possessions.

entries.section: (4) The love of money and entering the Kingdom of Heaven

paragraphs.text: Christ uncovered this ruler's sin, which was the love of money, and his heart was grieved because he could not sell his money and possessions for God's sake, and by this he judged himself unworthy of the Kingdom of Heaven. Ask yourself: are you ready, even if only in intention, to leave everything you have and keep your faith in God, or do you break the commandments while your heart is attached to material things? The practical application of leaving the love of money is a partial and gradual leaving, and giving tithes and even more than them, and doing works of mercy with everyone.

entries.section: (4) The love of money and entering the Kingdom of Heaven

paragraphs.text: Christ declared the seriousness of the problem of attachment to money, which prevents entering the Kingdom, because the rich often depend on their money and are attached to it. "How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!" And the only solution is that they trust in God alone and use their money for their living needs and for doing good, and are not troubled if they lose much of it. So what is meant is not that the rich do not enter the Kingdom, but those who trust in and are attached to their money.

entries.section: (4) The love of money and entering the Kingdom of Heaven

paragraphs.text: To show the impossibility of those who trust in their money entering the Kingdom, He gave a comparison: that a camel passing through the eye of a needle is easier than for one who trusts in his money to enter the Kingdom, that is, it is impossible for him to enter.

entries.section: (4) The love of money and entering the Kingdom of Heaven

paragraphs.text: Those who heard felt the difficulty of giving up the love of money, but Christ encouraged all the rich by saying that nothing is impossible with God, so that with His help the rich can be rid of their attachment to money.

entries.section: (4) The love of money and entering the Kingdom of Heaven

paragraphs.text: The disciples understood the importance of the rich leaving off the love of money, so Peter said on behalf of the disciples, "Lo, we have left all, and followed thee," though they had left nothing but worn-out nets, fishing boats and simple jobs which were their trades.

entries.section: (4) The love of money and entering the Kingdom of Heaven

paragraphs.text: Christ answered, showing His concern for anything a person leaves for His sake, whether material possessions or emotional relationships of attachment to family, friends and loved ones, for the sake of attachment to the love of God and His service. For God compensates him manifold in this life, that is, He gives him his material needs and health and gives him favor in the eyes of all. Like the monk who leaves a limited number of relatives, so his heart opens in love for everyone and all become his loved ones; and likewise the servant who gives up some of his time and rest and the enjoyment of his relationship with those close to him for the sake of serving Christ gains many souls and all become his loved ones, and then receives what cannot be expressed, which is the happiness of eternity. Look at God's graces that you receive in peace, joy and many blessings, and you will easily give up anything for the sake of His love.

entries.section: (5) Telling His disciples of His sufferings

paragraphs.text: Christ took His disciples apart to tell them of His sufferings which He would bear for the redemption of the world, these sufferings which the prophets had foretold, and He began to explain these prophecies to them, and that this would soon be fulfilled because they were heading toward Jerusalem, where all this would take place. And if Christ had spoken of leaving and detachment, He presents Himself as a practical example in leaving, even unto death, because of His love for us.

entries.section: (5) Telling His disciples of His sufferings

paragraphs.text: He explained to them how the Romans, that is, the Gentiles, would arrest Him, mock Him, beat Him and then kill Him, but He would rise from the dead on the third day.
If sufferings meet you, trust that blessings follow them, and the harder the sufferings, the more the blessings increase.

entries.section: (5) Telling His disciples of His sufferings

paragraphs.text: By this Christ wanted to prepare them to receive His sufferings, but they did not understand, because their minds were bound to the idea that Christ would be an earthly king; but after His resurrection they remembered all that He had told them and believed. Christ allowed this to be hidden from them so that they would not be alarmed and afraid, while remembering His words after the Resurrection helped them to believe.

entries.section: (6) The healing of the blind man on the way to Jericho

paragraphs.text: Christ was on His way to Jerusalem, and He passed through the city of Jericho, and there He found a blind man sitting by the way begging. Christ intended to pass by at this time in order to heal him, for He does good at all times, even while walking along the road.
The blind man heard the noise of a crowd approaching him, so he asked what this was, and they told him that Jesus Christ, with the crowds, was coming toward him.
If only you would seize every opportunity to do good, even on the road or in any place you enter: pray in every place, offer encouraging words to those you meet, and help everyone who asks you.

entries.section: (6) The healing of the blind man on the way to Jericho

paragraphs.text: The blind man believed that this was the awaited Messiah, the Son of David, and asked Him to have mercy on him; and because of his much crying out, the crowds in front tried to silence him so as not to trouble Christ, but he cried out and implored Christ all the more, showing a strong faith that could not be stopped.

The blind man signifies mankind, which lost its ability to see God, but if it believes in Christ and implores Him with faith and humility, it receives spiritual enlightenment and again enjoys the sight of God through the sacraments of the Church. As for the crowds in front, they signify the hindrances to faith: the lusts of the world, its preoccupations and all doubts, but God allows them to test faith, and then He pours out abundant blessings on His children.

entries.section: (6) The healing of the blind man on the way to Jericho

paragraphs.text: Christ stood and asked that the blind man be brought to Him, so they brought him near to Him, and Christ asked him, "What wilt thou that I shall do unto thee?", in order to affirm the importance of the human will and the spiritual striving evident in the continual crying out. The blind man said that he needed to be healed so that he might see, so Christ commanded with the authority of His divinity that he receive his sight, and his eyes were opened at once, and Christ declared the truth plainly, that the blind man's faith, which drove him in the striving of continual crying out and asking for healing, is what made Christ grant him the gift of sight.

entries.section: (6) The healing of the blind man on the way to Jericho

paragraphs.text: The blind man's heart was enlightened by faith before his bodily eyes were enlightened, and when Christ gave him healing he followed Him with the crowds, thanking God, and this thanksgiving of his became a motive for all the crowds to glorify and praise Christ.
Thank God at all times for His gifts, and in times of affliction too, and you will become a light in the world, encouraging everyone to a life of thanksgiving.
Zacchaeus, the parable of the faithful servants, Christ's entry into Jerusalem. The salvation of Zacchaeus (vv. 1-10):
1- And Jesus entered and passed through Jericho. 2- And, behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus, which was the chief among the publicans, and he was rich.

3- And he sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature. 4- And he ran before, and climbed up into a sycomore tree to see him: for he was to pass that way. 5- And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up, and saw him, and said unto him, "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." 6- And he made haste, and came down, and received him joyfully. 7- And when they saw it, they all murmured, saying, "That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner." 8- And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord, "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." 9- And Jesus said unto him, "This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham.
10- For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost."

entries.section: (6) The healing of the blind man on the way to Jericho

paragraphs.text: Christ entered Jericho with the crowds around Him, and a man who was one of the greatest rich men of Jericho heard of Him. He was Zacchaeus, whose name means "pure," and his office was chief of the tax collectors, that is, he paid the taxes for Jericho and all the villages around it, and then collected these Roman taxes arbitrarily and unjustly, gathering manifold amounts. So he was marked by cruelty and injustice along with great wealth.

He worked as a chief of the tax collectors, that is, one responsible for a group of tax collectors. The tax collectors collected more than they were entitled to, and so were marked by greed, wealth and cruelty in collecting taxes; how rich, then, how wicked and how far from God must their chief have been.
Zacchaeus was amazed by what he had heard of Christ's teachings and miracles, so he longed to see Him. This shows that God has a place in every heart, however far away it may seem.
Zacchaeus tried to see Jesus but could not because of the press of the crowd and because he was little of stature, so it became all the harder for him to break through the crowds to see Jesus.

When all Zacchaeus's attempts failed, he hit upon an idea, which was to climb a tree beside which Christ would pass. So he hurried and ran, forgetting his position and his wealth, and got ahead of the crowds until he reached a sycamore tree far along the road by which Christ would pass, and he climbed the tree like a boy, giving up his standing in society, and waited for Him to pass. The faith of Zacchaeus appeared clearly in his striving and his seeking to see Christ, and in his humility and his giving up his standing and his attempt to overcome every obstacle, whether the press of the crowd or his short stature.
Zacchaeus represents all sinners immersed in evil, yet the voice of God within them calls them, and if they respond with faith, their seeking appears in their search for Christ.

The sycamore tree signifies the Cross, and climbing it means bearing sufferings so that a person may see Christ in his life. It also signifies the Church, which the believer holds fast to and so sees Christ; and he must rise from earthly things to heavenly things through detachment and renunciation and love of prayer and contemplation, and then he is able to see God.

entries.section: (6) The healing of the blind man on the way to Jericho

paragraphs.text: The crowds did not distract Christ from looking at Zacchaeus, because He seeks those who are far off and every person who is ready for repentance. He even granted him the grace of entering his house and told him to hurry to do so. And He did not only enter but abode and lodged there.
If you take a step toward Christ, trust that He sees you, values your striving, helps you and grants you many blessings.

entries.section: (6) The healing of the blind man on the way to Jericho
